common_name: Maréchal Niel Rose (Golden Noisette Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or grafted plants in spring or fall against a sturdy structure with full sun; Maréchal Niel is a heat-loving Noisette that struggles in cold winters but is a classic performer across the Deep South, where its long canes need training and tying since it does not climb by twining.

directions: Plant against a fence, arbor, or pergola in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and tie the long, nearly thornless canes to their support as they grow since this Noisette climbs by producing long arching stems rather than by twining. Bred by Henri Pradel in France in 1864, Maréchal Niel produces large, deeply cupped, rich golden-yellow blooms that nod gracefully on weak necks and carry an intense, sweet tea fragrance, flowering heaviest in a big spring flush with lighter repeat through the growing season. It became one of the most treasured heirloom roses of the antebellum and Victorian South, where its vigorous growth and tolerance for heat and humidity made it a fixture on porches and arbors in a way it never could be in colder climates. Prune only lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape and remove dead wood, since flowers form on the previous year's growth.

common_name: Graham Thomas Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Graham Thomas grows as a large, arching shrub in most gardens but can be trained as a short climber to 10-12 feet in warm climates, making it flexible for a border, hedge, or trellis.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood; where grown as a climber, tie the long canes horizontally along a fence or trellis to maximize side-shoot flowering. Bred by David Austin and introduced in 1983, Graham Thomas was named for the renowned English rosarian and combines the rich, deep golden-yellow, cupped-to-rosette blooms and strong tea fragrance of an old garden rose with the vigor and repeat-flowering habit of a modern shrub rose. It quickly became one of the best-selling English roses ever introduced and remains a benchmark yellow rose for its combination of color saturation, fragrance, and reliable rebloom from late spring through frost. It shows good disease resistance in humid climates when given full sun and adequate air movement.

common_name: Abraham Darby Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun in rich, well-drained soil; Abraham Darby is a vigorous grower that can be kept as a large rounded shrub with regular pruning or allowed to reach 10-12 feet as a short climber against a wall or pillar in warm Southern gardens.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, compost-enriched soil and feed regularly through the growing season to support this heavy-blooming rose's vigorous repeat flowering. Bred by David Austin and named for the ironworks pioneer, Abraham Darby was introduced in 1985 and bears very large, deeply cupped blooms that open in warm blends of apricot, peach, and pink with a rich, fruity fragrance often compared to ripe peaches. Its vigorous, somewhat arching growth habit and strong disease resistance in humid conditions make it a dependable performer across the Gulf South, where it is frequently grown as a large shrub in a mixed border or trained up a pillar or low wall for extra height. Deadhead spent blooms through the season and prune hard in late winter to keep the shrub shapely and productive.

common_name: Climbing Pinkie Rose (Thornless Southern Heirloom Climber)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall against a fence, arbor, or mailbox post in full sun to partial shade; Climbing Pinkie is one of the most shade-tolerant and disease-resistant climbers available, tolerating a few hours less sun than most roses while still flowering well.

directions: Plant against a fence, arbor, or trellis in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained soil, and tie the long, nearly thornless, arching canes to their support as they grow. Discovered in 1952 as a climbing sport of the 1928 polyantha rose 'Pinkie', this heirloom produces large clusters of small, semi-double, clear rose-pink blooms in an overwhelming flush each spring with lighter sporadic rebloom through summer and fall. Its near-total lack of thorns, outstanding resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, and tolerance of poor soil and partial shade have made it a beloved pass-along rose throughout the Deep South for generations, often found scrambling over old fences and porches with no spray program at all. Prune immediately after the main spring bloom to shape and remove old wood, since next year's flowers form on canes grown this season.

common_name: Don Juan Rose (Velvet Red Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Set out grafted or own-root plants in spring or fall against a trellis, arbor, or pillar in full sun with good air circulation; Don Juan needs regular fungicide attention or careful site selection in humid Gulf South summers to keep blackspot in check, but rewards the effort with repeat flushes of classic red blooms.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil against a sturdy support, and train canes horizontally where possible to encourage more flowering side shoots along the length of the plant. Bred in Italy by Malandrone and introduced in 1958, Don Juan bears large, velvety, deep crimson-red blooms of classic high-centered hybrid-tea form carried on long stems, backed by a strong, sweet damask fragrance that makes it a favorite for cutting as well as climbing display. It repeat-blooms in flushes from late spring through fall and remains one of the most widely grown red climbing roses in American gardens for the richness of its color and scent, though it benefits from a preventive spray program or an airy site to manage blackspot in humid climates. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the plant vigorous and encourage strong new growth.
